18535.e: The Rhine is about 1,230 kilometres long. It is one of the longest rivers in Europe.
18535.m: The Rhine is about 1,200 kilometres long.

18536.q: Which river forms part of the border between Switzerland and Germany?
18536.e: Between Schaffhausen and Basel the Rhine often flows exactly along the border. Switzerland is on one side and Germany on the other.
18536.m: The Rhine is a border river with Germany.

18537.q: Which is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland?
18537.e: The Aare is almost 300 kilometres long. From its source to its mouth it flows only through Switzerland.
18537.m: The Aare is the longest river entirely in Switzerland.

18538.q: In which canton does the Aare rise?
18538.e: The Aare rises from glaciers in the Bernese Alps. That is near the Grimsel Pass.
18538.m: The Aare rises in the canton of Bern.

18539.q: Which river does the Aare flow into?
18539.e: At Koblenz in the canton of Aargau, the Aare flows into a bigger river. There it often carries more water than that river.
18539.m: The Aare flows into the Rhine.

18540.q: Which two lakes does the Aare flow through in the Bernese Oberland?
18540.e: The Aare first flows through Lake Brienz and then through Lake Thun. Interlaken lies between the lakes.
18540.m: The Aare flows through Lake Brienz and Lake Thun.

18541.q: Which town in the canton of Aargau gets its name from the Aare?
18541.e: Aarau lies on the Aare and is the capital of the canton of Aargau. The name Aargau also comes from the river.
18541.m: Aarau gets its name from the Aare.

18542.q: Which is the largest lake that Switzerland has a share in?
18542.e: Lake Geneva covers about 580 square kilometres. It has the shape of a crescent moon.
18542.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake on which Switzerland lies.

18543.q: What is Lake Geneva called in French?
18543.e: In French-speaking Switzerland, Lake Geneva is called “Lac Léman”. The name is very old.
18543.m: In French, Lake Geneva is called Lac Léman.

18544.q: Which country does Switzerland share Lake Geneva with?
18544.e: The north shore belongs to Switzerland, and a large part of the south shore to France. The border runs through the middle of the lake.
18544.m: Lake Geneva is also in France.

18545.q: Which river flows into Lake Geneva and out again?
18545.e: The Rhône comes from Valais into Lake Geneva. At the other end it flows on into France.
18545.m: The Rhône flows through Lake Geneva.

18546.q: Which castle stands right on the shore of Lake Geneva near Montreux?
18546.e: Chillon Castle stands on a rock in the water. It is one of the best-known castles in Switzerland.
18546.m: Chillon Castle stands on Lake Geneva.

18547.q: Which three countries border Lake Constance?
18547.e: Three countries meet at Lake Constance. Their shores all lie on the same lake.
18547.m: Three countries lie on Lake Constance.

18548.q: Which flower island is in Lake Constance?
18548.e: The island of Mainau is known for its many flowers and gardens. It belongs to Germany.
18548.m: Mainau is the flower island in Lake Constance.

18549.q: Which Swiss canton lies on Lake Constance?
18549.e: Thurgau has a long shore on Lake Constance. Places like Romanshorn and Kreuzlingen are there.

18550.q: Which big river flows into Lake Constance?
18550.e: The Rhine flows into Lake Constance in Austria, not far from Bregenz. It flows out again at Stein am Rhein.
18550.m: The Rhine flows through Lake Constance.

18551.q: What is the Bodensee called in English?
18551.e: In English the Bodensee is called “Lake Constance”. The name comes from the town of Konstanz on the lake.
18551.m: In English the Bodensee is called Lake Constance.

18552.q: How many centimes make one franc?
18552.e: One franc has 100 centimes. So two 50-centime coins together make one franc.

18553.q: Which is the largest Swiss banknote?
18553.e: The largest banknote in Switzerland is worth 1,000 francs (as of 2025). It is purple.
18553.m: The largest banknote is the 1,000-franc note.

18554.e: Every Swiss banknote has its own colour. The 50-franc note is green.

18555.q: You have 2 francs and 50 centimes. How many centimes is that?
18555.m: Two francs and fifty centimes are 250 centimes.

18556.q: Which national language do the most people in Switzerland speak?
18556.e: About 6 out of 10 people in Switzerland mainly speak German. In everyday life they mostly speak Swiss German.
18556.m: German is the most common language in Switzerland.

18557.q: Which national language is spoken almost only in the canton of the Grisons?
18557.e: Romansh is spoken almost only in the canton of the Grisons. It is the smallest national language.
18557.m: Romansh is spoken in the Grisons.

18558.q: What does the Italian word “Grazie” mean in English?
18558.e: You say “Grazie” to thank someone in Italian. In French you say “Merci”.

18559.q: What is the very long wooden musical instrument that is blown in the mountains called?
18559.e: The alphorn is often more than three metres long. In the past people used it to call across long distances in the mountains.
18559.m: The alphorn is a Swiss instrument.

18560.q: What is the Swiss sport called in which two men or women wrestle in sawdust?
18560.e: In Schwingen two people grab each other by short fabric trousers. Whoever puts the other on their back wins.
18560.m: In Schwingen people wrestle in sawdust.

18561.q: Which cheese dish is eaten together from one pot?
18561.e: For fondue, cheese melts in a pot. Everyone dips bread into it on long forks.
18561.m: Fondue is eaten together from one pot.

18562.q: Who visits children in Switzerland on 6 December?
18562.e: On 6 December Samichlaus, the Swiss Saint Nicholas, comes. He brings nuts, mandarins and gingerbread.

18563.q: What happens at the Alpabzug in autumn?
a: The cows come down from the alpine pasture to the valley
People ski down to the valley
People plant trees on the alpine pasture
People build huts on the alpine pasture
18563.e: In summer the cows are up on the alpine pasture. In autumn they are brought down to the valley, decorated with flowers and bells.
18563.m: At the Alpabzug the cows come down to the valley.

18564.q: What do people often light on hills and mountains on the evening of National Day?
18564.e: In the evening big fires burn on many hills. They are called bonfires on the heights.

18565.q: What do children often carry through the streets on the evening of 1 August?
18565.e: Lampions are colourful paper lanterns. They are often painted with Swiss crosses.

18566.e: In the Federal Charter of 1291 three valley communities promised to help each other. This is seen as the beginning of the Swiss Confederation.

18567.q: The Rütli meadow is an important place for 1 August. Which lake is it on?
18567.e: The Rütli meadow is in the canton of Uri, high above Lake Lucerne. Many people visit it on National Day.
18567.m: The Rütli is on Lake Lucerne.

18568.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Ticino?
18568.e: Lugano is the largest town in Ticino, but the capital is Bellinzona with its three castles.
18568.m: The capital of Ticino is Bellinzona, not Lugano.

18569.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Valais?
18569.e: The capital of Valais is called Sion in French and Sitten in German.
18569.m: Sion, Sitten in German, is the capital of Valais.

18570.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Jura?
18570.e: The youngest canton in Switzerland has Delémont as its capital.
18570.m: Delémont is the capital of the canton of Jura.

18571.q: Where are the government and parliament of the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden based?
18571.e: Herisau is the seat of the government and cantonal parliament of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. Appenzell is the capital of the neighbouring canton of Innerrhoden.
18571.m: Herisau is the seat of government of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

18572.q: Which place is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden?
18572.e: Stans is the capital of Nidwalden, and Sarnen that of Obwalden.
18572.m: Stans is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden.

18573.q: Which region lies between the Jura and the Alps and is the most densely populated?
18573.e: On the Swiss Plateau, between Lake Geneva and Lake Constance, are most of the big cities, and most people live there.
18573.m: Most people in Switzerland live on the Swiss Plateau.

18574.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland's area belongs to the Alps?
18574.e: The Alps and Pre-Alps together cover about three fifths of Switzerland, the Swiss Plateau almost a third and the Jura about a tenth.
18574.m: About three fifths of Switzerland lies in the Alps.

18575.q: What is the French-speaking part of Switzerland called?
18575.e: French-speaking western Switzerland is called Romandie.
18575.m: The French-speaking west of Switzerland is called Romandie.

18576.q: In which canton is Romansh used as an official language?
18576.e: The Grisons has three languages: German, Italian and Romansh.
18576.m: Romansh is an official language in the canton of the Grisons.

18577.q: In which canton is Italian the only official language?
18577.e: Ticino is the only canton where Italian is the only official language.
18577.m: In Ticino, Italian is the only official language.

18578.q: What is the region with the cantons of Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden and Zug called?
18578.e: Central Switzerland lies around Lake Lucerne. The founding cantons of the Confederation are also here.
18578.m: Lucerne, Uri and Schwyz belong to Central Switzerland.

18579.q: With which neighbouring country does Switzerland have the longest border?
18579.e: At more than 700 kilometres, the border with Italy is Switzerland's longest national border.
18579.m: Switzerland's longest border is the one with Italy.

18580.q: With which neighbouring country does Switzerland have the shortest border?
18580.e: The border with Liechtenstein is only about 41 kilometres long and mostly follows the Rhine.
18580.m: Switzerland's shortest national border is the one with Liechtenstein.

18581.q: Which currency do people pay with in Liechtenstein?
18581.e: Liechtenstein has no currency of its own and has used the Swiss franc since 1924.
18581.m: In Liechtenstein people also pay with Swiss francs.

18582.q: Which neighbouring country does the canton of Geneva border?
18582.e: The canton of Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France and is linked to Vaud only by a narrow strip.
18582.m: The canton of Geneva is almost entirely surrounded by France.

18583.q: Which mountain massif does the highest peak in Switzerland belong to?
18583.e: The highest Swiss peak is the main summit of the Monte Rosa massif in Valais.
18583.m: The highest peak in Switzerland belongs to the Monte Rosa massif.

18584.q: Which mountain range lies in the north-west of Switzerland along the border with France?
18584.e: The Jura is a limestone mountain range that stretches from Geneva to Schaffhausen.
18584.m: The Jura lies in the north-west of Switzerland.

18585.q: Which Alpine pass links the canton of Uri with Ticino?
18585.e: The Gotthard Pass leads from Andermatt in the canton of Uri to Airolo in Ticino.
18585.m: The Gotthard Pass links Uri with Ticino.

18586.q: Which is the longest river that runs entirely within Switzerland?
18586.e: The Aare is 288 kilometres long and flows from the Bernese Alps to where it joins the Rhine at Koblenz in Aargau.
18586.m: The Aare is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland.

18587.q: Which river from the Engadine carries its water via the Danube to the Black Sea?
18587.e: The Inn rises in the Engadine, flows through Austria and joins the Danube at Passau.
18587.m: The Inn carries water from the Engadine all the way to the Black Sea.

18588.q: Which sea does the water of the Ticino reach?
18588.e: The Ticino flows through Lake Maggiore into the Po, which flows into the Adriatic.
18588.m: The Ticino drains via the Po into the Adriatic.

18590.q: Which is the largest lake that lies entirely within Switzerland?
18590.e: Lake Neuchâtel covers about 215 square kilometres and lies entirely on Swiss soil.
18590.m: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake entirely in Switzerland.

18591.q: Which is the largest lake that Switzerland has a share in?
18591.e: Lake Geneva covers about 580 square kilometres. Almost 60 per cent of it belongs to Switzerland, and the rest, with most of the south shore, to France.
18591.m: Lake Geneva is the largest lake with a Swiss share.

18592.q: Apart from Switzerland, which countries lie on Lake Constance?
18592.e: Switzerland, Germany and Austria meet at Lake Constance.
18592.m: Three countries border each other at Lake Constance.

18593.q: Which lake lies partly in Switzerland and partly in Italy?
18593.e: The northern part of Lake Maggiore, with Locarno, belongs to Switzerland, and the larger part to Italy.
18593.m: Lake Maggiore lies in Switzerland and Italy.

18594.q: Which town lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz?
18594.e: The name Interlaken means “between the lakes”.
18594.m: Interlaken lies between Lake Thun and Lake Brienz.

18595.q: For how many years is the Federal Council elected?
18595.e: The Federal Council is elected for a four-year term after each general election of the National Council.
18595.m: The Federal Council's term of office is four years.

18596.q: How long does the office of President of the Swiss Confederation last?
18596.e: Each year one member of the Federal Council becomes President of the Confederation and chairs the meetings.
18596.m: The presidency of the Confederation changes every year.

18597.q: What is the sharing of Federal Council seats that applied from 1959 to 2003 called?
18597.e: The magic formula shared the seven seats among the four largest parties in the ratio 2 to 2 to 2 to 1.
18597.m: The magic formula shared the Federal Council seats among the large parties.

18598.q: What does the number of National Council seats a canton has depend on?
a: on the age of the canton
18598.e: The 200 seats are shared among the cantons according to their population.
18598.m: Large cantons have more seats in the National Council than small ones.

18599.q: What is the minimum number of National Council seats each canton has?
18599.e: The Federal Constitution guarantees every canton at least one seat in the National Council, even if it has few inhabitants.
18599.m: Every canton has at least one seat in the National Council.

18600.q: Which canton has the most members of the National Council?
18600.e: As the canton with the largest population, Zurich has had 36 seats since the 2023 elections.
18600.m: Zurich has the most seats in the National Council.

18601.q: In which building does the National Council meet?
a: in the Federal Palace in Bern
in the Town Hall in Zurich
in the Palais des Nations in Geneva
in the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne
18601.e: The National Council and the Council of States meet in the parliament building of the Federal Palace in Bern.
18601.m: Parliament meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.

18602.q: How many ordinary sessions does parliament hold each year?
18602.e: There are the spring, summer, autumn and winter sessions, which usually last three weeks each.
18602.m: Parliament meets for four ordinary sessions every year.

18603.q: How many members of the Council of States does the canton of Basel-Stadt have?
18603.e: The former half-cantons, such as Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, each have one member in the Council of States.
18603.m: Basel-Stadt has one seat in the Council of States.

18604.q: Who decides how the members of the Council of States are elected?
18604.e: Elections to the Council of States are regulated by each canton. Most cantons use a majority voting system.
18604.m: Each canton decides for itself how its members of the Council of States are elected.

18605.q: What else is the Council of States called?
18605.e: With 46 members, the Council of States is the smaller of the two chambers of parliament and represents the cantons.
18605.m: The Council of States is the small chamber and represents the cantons.

18606.q: What is needed for parliament to pass a new federal law?
a: The Council of States decides alone.
18606.e: The National Council and the Council of States have equal rights. A law is only passed if both chambers agree on the same text.
18606.m: A federal law needs the approval of the National Council and the Council of States.

18607.q: Since which year have women in Switzerland been allowed to vote and stand for election at federal level?
18607.e: On 7 February 1971 the men voted in favour of women's right to vote and stand for election at federal level.
18607.m: Since 1971 women have had the right to vote at federal level.

18608.q: Which canton was the last to introduce women's right to vote at cantonal level?
18608.e: In 1990 the Federal Supreme Court forced Appenzell Innerrhoden to give women the right to vote in the canton.
18608.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to introduce women's right to vote, in 1990.

18609.q: On which three political levels is Switzerland built?
18609.e: In Swiss federalism, the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities each have their own tasks.
18609.m: Switzerland is made up of the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities.

18610.q: What does a popular initiative need in order to be approved?
a: A majority of the people and of the cantons
Only a majority of the people
Only a majority of the cantons
The approval of the Federal Council
18610.e: Because a popular initiative changes the constitution, both the majority of voters and the majority of the cantons must agree.
18610.m: A popular initiative needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

18611.q: What must the people always vote on?
a: on changes to the Federal Constitution
on the election of the Federal Council
18611.e: Changes to the constitution are subject to a mandatory referendum. People only vote on laws if a referendum is called.
18611.m: Every change to the Federal Constitution is put to the people.

18612.q: On how many dates per year are federal votes usually held?
18612.e: The Federal Council usually sets four voting Sundays each year.
18612.m: There are usually four federal voting Sundays each year.

18613.q: Which canton was the first to introduce a voting age of 16 in 2007?
18613.e: In 2007 the Landsgemeinde in Glarus decided that young people from the age of 16 may have a say in the canton.
18613.m: In 2007 Glarus became the first canton with a voting age of 16.

18614.q: How many cantonal votes are there in total in a vote?
18614.e: Twenty cantons have a full cantonal vote and six cantons have half a vote. 20 plus 6 times 0.5 makes 23.
18614.m: There are 23 cantonal votes in total.

18615.q: In which year will the next general election of the National Council take place (as of 2026)?
18615.e: The National Council is elected every four years. After the 2023 election, the next one follows in autumn 2027.
18615.m: The National Council is elected every four years.

18616.q: Which system is used to elect the National Council in most cantons?
18616.e: With proportional representation, parties get seats in proportion to their votes. Only cantons with one seat use majority voting.
18616.m: The National Council is mostly elected by proportional representation.

18617.q: What is it called when you write names of candidates from other lists onto an election list?
18617.e: With panachage you mix candidates from different parties on one list.
18617.m: Mixing names from different lists is called panachage.

18618.q: Which party won the largest share of the vote in the 2023 National Council elections?
18618.e: In 2023 the SVP won about 28 per cent of the vote and remained the party with the most voters.
18618.m: The SVP was the strongest party in 2023.

18619.q: In which year did Switzerland get its first Federal Constitution?
18619.e: With the Federal Constitution of 1848, Switzerland changed from a confederation of states into a federal state.
18619.m: Switzerland has been a federal state since 1848.

18620.q: Since when has today's Federal Constitution been in force?
18620.e: The people and the cantons approved the new constitution in 1999. It came into force on 1 January 2000.
18620.m: Today's Federal Constitution has been in force since 2000.

18621.q: What is the most important law in Switzerland, which also contains the fundamental rights, called?
18621.e: The Federal Constitution stands above all other laws. It sets out the fundamental rights and how the state is organised.
18621.m: The Federal Constitution is the most important law in Switzerland.

18622.q: How many national languages does the Federal Constitution name?
18622.e: Article 4 names German, French, Italian and Romansh as national languages.

18623.q: What is Bern officially called as the seat of the Federal Council and parliament?
18623.e: Officially, Switzerland has no capital. Bern is the federal city.
18623.m: Bern is officially the federal city of Switzerland.

18624.q: At which congress was Switzerland's neutrality recognised by the great powers in 1815?
18624.e: At the Congress of Vienna after the Napoleonic Wars, the European powers recognised Switzerland's permanent neutrality.
18624.m: Switzerland's neutrality was recognised at the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

18625.q: Which organisation is neutral Switzerland NOT a member of?
18625.e: As a neutral state, Switzerland does not belong to any military alliance.
18625.m: Neutral Switzerland does not belong to any military alliance.

18626.q: What are neutral Switzerland's mediation work and protecting power mandates called?
18626.e: Through its good offices, Switzerland mediates between states or represents countries that have no relations with each other.
18626.m: Through its good offices, Switzerland helps to mediate in conflicts.

18627.q: After which defeat in 1515 did the Confederation withdraw from the wars of the great powers?
18627.e: After the defeat at Marignano in northern Italy, the Confederates gave up playing power politics. This is seen as the beginning of neutrality.
18627.m: After Marignano in 1515, Switzerland began to stay out of foreign wars.

18628.q: Which three communities made the Federal Charter in 1291?
18628.e: The Federal Charter of early August 1291 is seen as the founding document of the Confederation.
18628.m: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden made the Federal Charter in 1291.

18629.q: In which year did the Battle of Morgarten take place?
18629.e: At Morgarten in 1315, the men of Schwyz defeated a Habsburg army.
18629.m: The Battle of Morgarten was in 1315.

18630.q: According to legend, which hero sacrificed himself in the Battle of Sempach in 1386?
18630.e: According to legend, Winkelried grabbed the enemy's lances and so opened a gap for the Confederates.
18630.m: Arnold Winkelried is the legendary hero of the Battle of Sempach.

18631.q: What was the unitary state that the French set up in Switzerland in 1798 called?
18631.e: After the French invasion, the Helvetic Republic replaced the Old Swiss Confederacy from 1798 to 1803.
18631.m: The Helvetic Republic was created in 1798 under French influence.

18632.q: What is Switzerland's last civil war of 1847 called?
18632.e: In the Sonderbund War the liberal cantons defeated seven Catholic conservative cantons.
18632.m: The Sonderbund War of 1847 was Switzerland's last civil war.

18633.q: According to legend, in which place did William Tell shoot the apple off his son's head?
18633.e: On the village square of Altdorf in the canton of Uri, a monument recalls the apple shot.
18633.m: William Tell's apple shot took place in Altdorf.

18634.q: Which man from Geneva founded the Red Cross and received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901?
18634.e: Henry Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859 and then proposed founding the Red Cross.
18634.m: Henry Dunant is the founder of the Red Cross.

18635.q: Which writer wrote the stories about “Heidi”?
18635.e: Johanna Spyri from Hirzel published the Heidi books in 1880 and 1881.
18635.m: Johanna Spyri is the author of “Heidi”.

18636.q: Which physicist developed the special theory of relativity in Bern in 1905?
18636.e: Einstein was working at the patent office in Bern at the time and published several groundbreaking papers in 1905.
18636.m: Albert Einstein developed the theory of relativity in Bern.

18637.q: Which world-famous architect comes from La Chaux-de-Fonds?
18637.e: Le Corbusier's real name was Charles-Édouard Jeanneret. Several of his buildings are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
18637.m: Le Corbusier was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds.

18638.q: How many Grand Slam singles titles did Roger Federer win?
18638.e: Between 2003 and 2018 Federer won twenty Grand Slam singles tournaments, eight of them at Wimbledon.
18638.m: Roger Federer won 20 Grand Slam titles.

18639.q: Which educator from Zurich wanted children to learn with “head, heart and hand”?
18639.e: Around 1800 Pestalozzi worked for the education of poor children and shaped state schooling.
18639.m: Pestalozzi wanted children to learn with head, heart and hand.

18640.q: In which town does the food company Nestlé have its headquarters?
18640.e: Nestlé has its headquarters in Vevey on Lake Geneva.

18641.e: Gottlieb Duttweiler first sold goods from lorries. Later he turned Migros into cooperatives.

18642.q: What does the abbreviation SBB stand for?
18642.e: Swiss Federal Railways was formed in 1902 from several private railway companies.
18642.m: SBB stands for Swiss Federal Railways.

18643.q: In which city do the pharmaceutical companies Roche and Novartis have their headquarters?
18643.e: Basel is the centre of the Swiss pharmaceutical and chemical industry.

18644.q: Which industry is especially important in the Jura arc from Geneva to Schaffhausen?
18644.e: Places such as La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle and Biel are known worldwide for making watches.
18644.m: Many Swiss watches are made in the Jura arc.

18645.q: What did an engineer from French-speaking Switzerland invent after finding burrs in his dog's fur?
18645.e: George de Mestral saw how the tiny hooks of the burrs held on to the fur. Using this as a model, he made the hook-and-loop fastener, known as Velcro, and patented it in 1951.
18645.m: The hook-and-loop fastener was invented in Switzerland.

18646.q: Which kitchen tool from Switzerland is called “Rex”?
18646.e: The “Rex” peeler was invented in Switzerland in 1947. With its moving blade you can peel potatoes and carrots thinly.
18646.m: The “Rex” peeler is a Swiss invention.

18647.q: Which sweet was invented in 1875 in Vevey on Lake Geneva?
18647.e: Daniel Peter was the first to mix condensed milk into chocolate. This created milk chocolate, for which Switzerland is famous.
18647.m: Milk chocolate was invented in Switzerland.

18648.q: What is the see-through film called that a Swiss chemist invented in 1908?
18648.e: Jacques Brandenberger wanted to make a tablecloth that stains would not stick to. In doing so he invented the see-through film cellophane.

18649.q: Which world-famous tool did Karl Elsener from Ibach in Schwyz have made for the army from 1891?
18649.e: Karl Elsener supplied the Swiss army with soldiers' knives. In 1897 he developed the officer's knife, which is known all over the world today.
18649.m: The Swiss Army knife comes from Ibach in Schwyz.

18748.q: What is the most important source of light for the Earth?
18748.e: The sun shines by itself and sends light and heat to the Earth. Without it, the Earth would be dark and freezing cold.
18748.m: The sun is our most important source of light.

18749.q: Why does the moon shine at night?
18749.e: The moon does not shine by itself. It is lit up by the sun and reflects this light back to us.
18749.m: The moon only shines because the sun lights it up.

18750.q: Which object reflects almost all light, so that you can see yourself in it?
18750.e: A mirror is very smooth and shiny. That is why it reflects light in a way that creates a reflection.

18751.q: What can you use to see a small ant much bigger?
18751.e: A magnifying glass is a curved piece of glass. It bends the light so that small things look much bigger.
18751.m: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger.

18752.q: How does light travel when nothing is in the way?
18752.e: Light travels in straight lines. That is why you cannot see round a corner.
18752.m: Light always travels in a straight line.

18753.q: Which is faster, light or sound?
18753.e: In a thunderstorm you see the lightning first and only hear the thunder later. Light is much faster than sound.
18753.m: Light is much faster than sound.

18755.q: When is your shadow shortest outdoors?
18755.e: At midday the sun is at its highest in the sky. Then the light falls steeply and the shadow is short.
18755.m: Your shadow is shortest at midday.

18756.q: The sun is in the east. Which way does your shadow point?
18756.e: The shadow is always on the side facing away from the light source. If the sun is in the east, it points west.
18756.m: The shadow always points away from the light source.

18757.q: What happens to the shadow when you move closer to the torch?
18757.e: The closer an object is to the torch, the more light it blocks. That is why its shadow on the wall gets bigger.
18757.m: Close to the torch, the shadow gets bigger.

18758.q: Which object casts almost no shadow?
18758.e: Clear glass lets most light through. That is why there is almost no shadow behind it.
18758.m: Transparent things hardly cast a shadow.

18759.q: Which old device shows the time with a shadow?
18759.e: On a sundial, a rod casts a shadow. Because the sun moves across the sky, the shadow points to different hours during the day.
18759.m: A sundial shows the time with a shadow.

18760.q: Why is there hardly any shadow on a dull, cloudy day?
a: The moon is in the way
18760.e: The clouds spread the sunlight in all directions. Because the light comes from everywhere, no clear shadow forms.
18760.m: When it is cloudy, the light is spread out and shadows are weak.

18761.q: Which device do you use to measure how warm something is?
18761.e: A thermometer shows the temperature. In Switzerland it is measured in degrees Celsius.

18762.q: Which spoon gets warm fastest in hot tea?
18762.e: Metal conducts heat very well. Wood and plastic conduct heat badly and so stay cool for longer.

18763.q: Why do you wear a woolly jumper in winter?
a: It keeps in your body heat
18763.e: Wool traps lots of air. This air lets your body heat escape only slowly.
18763.m: A jumper keeps your body heat close to you.

18764.q: What happens to chocolate in the hot sun?
18764.e: The heat makes solid chocolate soft and runny. This process is called melting.

18765.q: What happens when you rub your hands together quickly?
18765.e: Rubbing creates friction. Friction produces heat, so your hands get warm.

18766.q: Which colour gets hottest in the sun?
18766.e: Black things absorb almost all the sunlight and so get hot. White things reflect a lot of light and stay cooler.
18766.m: Dark colours get hotter in the sun than light ones.

18767.q: At how many degrees Celsius does water freeze?
18767.e: Pure water turns into ice at 0 degrees Celsius. That is why there is ice on the puddles when it is below zero.

18768.q: What does water become when it freezes?
18768.e: When water gets cold enough, it becomes solid. Frozen water is called ice.

18769.q: What happens to an ice cube in a warm room?
18769.e: The warm air gives heat to the ice cube. This makes the ice liquid again.
18769.m: Ice melts into water in the warmth.

18770.q: Why does an ice cube float in water?
a: Ice is lighter than the same amount of water
18770.e: Ice is a little lighter than the same amount of liquid water. That is why it floats on top, just like icebergs in the sea.
18770.m: Ice floats because it is lighter than water.

18771.q: Why can a full glass bottle burst in the freezer?
18771.e: Water needs more space as ice than as a liquid. The ice then pushes so hard that the bottle can burst.

18772.q: What do you need a fridge for?
a: To keep food fresh for longer
18772.e: Germs multiply much more slowly in the cold. That is why milk and vegetables stay fresh for longer in the fridge.
18772.m: Cold keeps food fresh for longer.

18773.q: What does an object have to do to make a sound?
18773.e: Sounds are made when something moves quickly back and forth. You can see this well on a plucked guitar string.

18774.q: Which part of the body do we hear with?
18774.e: The ears catch the sound. The brain turns it into noises, music and speech.

18775.q: What do you hear when you shout loudly in the mountains and your shout comes back?
18775.e: The sound bounces off a rock face and comes back. This reflected sound is called an echo.

18776.q: Why can you not hear any sounds in space?
a: Everything is too far away there
18776.e: Sound needs air, water or a solid material to travel through. In space there is almost nothing, so sound cannot travel.

18777.q: Which animal uses the echo of its calls to fly in the dark?
18777.e: Bats give out very high-pitched calls. From the echo they can detect obstacles and insects, even at night.
18777.m: Bats find their way using echoes.

18778.q: What protects your ears from very loud noise?
18778.e: Very loud noises can damage your ears permanently. Ear protection muffles the noise.
18778.m: Ear protection protects your ears from loud noise.

18779.q: A thunderstorm is about 1 kilometre away. How long after the lightning do you hear the thunder?
18779.e: Sound travels around one kilometre in about 3 seconds. If you count the seconds between lightning and thunder, you can estimate the distance.
18779.m: About 3 seconds between lightning and thunder means around 1 kilometre.

18780.q: What does a ball that is lying still need to make it roll?
18780.e: A ball that is lying still stays where it is. Only a push or a nudge gets it moving.
18780.m: Without a push, a ball lying still stays where it is.

18781.q: Why does a ball on the grass soon stop rolling?
18781.e: The grass keeps slowing the ball down a little. This braking effect is called friction.

18782.q: On which surface do you slip most easily?
18782.e: Ice is very smooth and has little friction. That is why your feet slip on it easily.
18782.m: There is little friction on smooth ice.

18783.q: Why do passengers fall forwards when the bus suddenly brakes?
a: Their body wants to keep going
18783.e: Your body moves along with the bus. If the bus suddenly brakes, your body wants to keep going forwards. That is why you should hold on tight.
18783.m: In a braking bus, your body wants to keep going.

18784.q: Why does a bike tyre have a tread with grooves?
18784.e: The grooves grip the ground better, especially on gravel, earth or snow. This means the bike does not slip so easily.
18784.m: Grooves in the tyre give more grip.

18785.q: What does a swing do when you give it one push?
18785.e: A swing is a pendulum. It swings back and forth until friction slowly stops it.
18785.m: A swing swings back and forth.

18786.q: In which unit does the speedometer in a car show the speed?
18786.e: The speedometer shows how many kilometres the car would travel in one hour. This is written as km/h.
18786.m: In a car, speed is measured in kilometres per hour.

18787.q: Which animal is the fastest on land?
18787.e: The cheetah can run at around 100 kilometres per hour for a short time. No other land animal is as fast.
18787.m: The cheetah is the fastest land animal.

18788.q: What is the maximum speed a car may drive on a motorway in Switzerland?
18788.e: On Swiss motorways the speed limit is normally 120 kilometres per hour.
18788.m: On Swiss motorways the limit is usually 120.

18789.q: What is the usual maximum speed for a car in built-up areas in Switzerland?
18789.e: In built-up areas in Switzerland the basic speed limit is 50. In some neighbourhoods it is even 30.
18789.m: In villages and towns the limit is usually 50.

18790.q: Lea runs 100 metres in 20 seconds, Tim in 25 seconds. Who is faster?
18790.e: Both run the same distance. Whoever needs less time is faster, and that is Lea with 20 seconds.
18790.m: Whoever needs less time for the same distance is faster.

18791.q: A bike travels 15 kilometres in one hour. How far does it get in 2 hours at the same speed?
18791.e: Every hour the bike travels 15 kilometres. In 2 hours that is 15 + 15 = 30 kilometres.
18791.m: Riding twice as long means getting twice as far.

18792.q: What happens to a ball that you throw high into the air?
18792.e: The ball gets slower and slower as it flies up and then turns round. The Earth pulls it back down again.
18792.m: What you throw up falls back down.

18793.q: Which falls to the ground more slowly through the air?
18793.e: The air strongly slows down the flat, light sheet. That is why it floats down slowly while the stone falls quickly.
18793.m: Air slows down light, flat things as they fall.

18794.q: Who, according to a story about a falling apple, made gravity famous?
18794.e: Isaac Newton was an English scientist. He described how the same force makes the apple fall and keeps the moon going round the Earth.

18795.q: What is jumping like on the moon?
18795.e: The moon pulls much more weakly than the Earth. That is why astronauts could make high jumps there.
18795.m: Gravity is weaker on the moon than on Earth.

18796.q: What do bathroom scales show when you stand on them?
18796.e: Gravity presses your body onto the scales. The scales then show how heavy you are, in kilograms.
18796.m: Scales show how heavy something is.

18797.q: Why does a parachutist fall slowly?
a: The parachute brakes in the air
18797.e: The large canopy catches a lot of air. The air slows down the fall, but gravity keeps working.
18797.m: A parachute slows the fall using air.

18798.q: What are the two ends of a magnet called?
18798.e: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. That is where the force is strongest.
18798.m: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

18800.q: Which device uses a magnet to show direction?
18800.e: The needle in a compass is a small magnet. It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field and points north.

18801.q: Which object is NOT attracted by a magnet?
18801.e: Copper is a metal that a magnet does not attract. Nails, screws and paper clips contain iron.
18801.m: Not all metals are attracted by magnets.

18802.q: Can a magnet work through a sheet of paper?
18802.e: The force of a magnet also works through paper, glass or thin wood. If you put a sheet of paper over a paper clip, the magnet can still move it.
18802.m: Magnetic force also works through paper.

18803.q: What are small magnets often used for at home?
18803.e: Fridge magnets hold notes and pictures on the door. The outside of the door is usually a steel sheet that the magnet attracts.
18803.m: Fridge magnets stick to the steel door.

18804.q: What does a circuit need for a bulb to light up?
18804.e: Electricity only flows when the circuit is closed all the way round. If it is broken, the bulb stays dark.
18804.m: Electricity only flows in a closed circuit.

18805.q: What is the inside of a cable usually made of?
18805.e: Copper conducts electricity very well. That is why inside the cable there is a copper wire covered with plastic.
18805.m: In a cable, a copper wire usually carries the electricity.

18806.q: Why is a cable covered with plastic?
18806.e: Plastic is an insulator; it does not let electricity through. This means you can touch the cable safely.
18806.m: The plastic covering protects you from electricity.

a: Put your fingers in a socket
18807.e: Electricity at high voltage comes out of a socket. This is extremely dangerous, so you never put anything into it.
18807.m: Sockets are dangerous and not a toy.

18808.q: What is a light switch for?
a: It opens and closes the circuit
18808.e: When you press the switch, the circuit is closed and the light comes on. When you press it again, the circuit is broken.
18808.m: A switch opens and closes the circuit.

18809.q: What is lightning in a thunderstorm?
18809.e: Lightning is an enormous electrical discharge between clouds or between a cloud and the ground. It is very hot and dangerous.
18809.m: Lightning is a huge electric spark.

18810.q: What protects a house from a lightning strike in a thunderstorm?
18810.e: A lightning conductor is a metal rod with a wire leading into the ground. If lightning strikes, it carries the electricity safely into the earth.
18810.m: A lightning conductor carries lightning safely into the earth.

18811.e: A battery stores energy chemically. When it is connected, it gives off electricity.
18811.m: A battery stores energy for electricity.

18812.q: What are the two terminals of a battery called?
18812.e: Every battery has a positive terminal and a negative terminal. You have to put it into the device the right way round.
18812.m: A battery has a positive and a negative terminal.

18813.e: Batteries contain substances that harm the environment. In Switzerland you take them back to a shop or a collection point.
18813.m: You take flat batteries to a collection point.

18814.q: What do you call a battery that can be recharged?
18814.e: A rechargeable battery can be charged again with a charger. Mobile phones and tablets have one.
18814.m: A rechargeable battery can be charged again.

18815.q: Which device often works with batteries?
18815.e: A torch has to be something you can carry around. That is why it gets its electricity from batteries instead of a socket.

18816.q: What happens when a battery is flat?
18816.e: A flat battery no longer gives off electricity. Then the device needs a new battery or has to be recharged.
18816.m: Without electricity from the battery, the device does not work.

18817.q: What helps you get a heavy box onto a lorry more easily?
18817.e: You push the box up a ramp, which is a sloping surface. The way is longer, but you need less force.
18817.m: A ramp saves force, but the way gets longer.

18818.q: Which simple machine is used to raise a flag up a pole?
18818.e: At the top of the flagpole there is a pulley. You pull the rope downwards and the flag goes up.
18818.m: With a pulley you can pull downwards to lift something up.

18819.q: Which tool is a wedge that you use to split wood?
18819.e: The blade of an axe is thin at the front and thick at the back. Like a wedge, it pushes the wood apart.
18819.m: An axe splits wood like a wedge.

18820.q: Why do mountain roads wind up the slope in bends?
a: So that it is less steep
18820.e: A road with bends is like a long sloping surface. The way gets longer but less steep, which saves force.
18820.m: A longer way makes a climb less steep.

18821.q: Which simple machine is a screw?
a: A sloping surface wound round a rod
A small wheel without an axle
18821.e: The thread of a screw is like a sloping surface wound round a rod. This lets it go into wood with little force.
18821.m: A screw thread is a sloping surface wound round a rod.

18822.e: With a lever, pulley, wedge or sloping surface you need less force. This makes it easier to move heavy things.
18822.m: Simple machines make heavy work easier.

18823.q: Which tool do you use to turn a screw into wood?
18823.e: The handle of a screwdriver is thicker than its tip. That is why you can turn the screw with little force.
18823.m: You turn screws into wood with a screwdriver.

18824.q: Which piece of playground equipment is a lever?
18824.e: A seesaw is a long board that rests on a pivot in the middle. That is exactly how a lever works.

18825.q: A heavy child and a light child are on a seesaw. Where must the heavy child sit?
18825.e: Whoever is heavier sits closer to the middle. This makes the seesaw balance.
18825.m: The heavier child sits closer to the middle of the seesaw.

18826.q: Which part of your body works like a lever?
18826.e: The forearm turns at the elbow like a lever. The muscles pull on it and so lift things up.
18826.m: Your arm works like a lever.

18827.e: A pair of scissors consists of two levers with a shared pivot in the middle. That is why they cut with little force.

18828.q: What is the easiest way to open a tight lid on a paint tin?
a: With a screwdriver as a lever
18828.e: You put the screwdriver under the edge and push on the handle. The long handle acting as a lever makes the force big.
18828.m: A long lever makes it easier to prise something open.

18829.q: Where do you have to push to open a heavy door most easily?
a: In the middle at the bottom
18829.e: The door turns on its hinges. The further away you push, the less force you need.
18829.m: Far from the pivot you need less force.

18830.q: Which device lifts a heavy load with a lever and a wheel?
18830.e: On a wheelbarrow the wheel is the pivot. You lift the long handles and can carry a lot.
18830.m: A wheelbarrow is a lever with a wheel.

18831.q: Why was the invention of the wheel so important?
a: Things can be moved more easily
18831.e: A wheel rolls and does not slide over the ground. That is why much less force is needed to transport loads.
18831.m: Wheels make transporting things much easier.

18832.q: What is the rod that a wheel turns around called?
18832.e: A wheel sits on an axle and turns around it. On a car, the axle connects two wheels.
18832.m: A wheel turns around an axle.

18833.q: What are the thin rods in a bike wheel called?
18833.e: Spokes connect the middle of the wheel to the rim. They make the wheel strong and yet light.
18833.m: The spokes make the bike wheel strong.

18834.q: On a bike, what connects the pedals to the back wheel?
18834.e: When you push the pedals, the chain moves. It drives the back wheel.
18834.m: The bike chain passes the force on to the back wheel.

18835.q: What do you call wheels with teeth that fit into each other?
18835.e: Gearwheels fit into each other with their teeth. When one turns, the others turn with it, for example in a clock.
18835.m: Gearwheels fit into each other and turn together.

18836.q: What does a rack railway such as the Pilatus Railway have between the rails?
18836.e: The train's gearwheels fit into the toothed rack. This lets the train travel up very steep stretches without slipping. The Pilatus Railway is the steepest rack railway in the world.
18836.m: Rack railways climb steep mountains thanks to a toothed rack.

18837.q: Where does your body get energy from?
18837.e: Food contains energy. The body needs it to grow, move, think and keep warm.
18837.m: Our body gets energy from food.

18838.q: Which power station uses the power of water?
18838.e: In a hydroelectric power station, flowing or falling water drives a turbine. In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower.
18838.m: In Switzerland a lot of electricity comes from hydropower.

18839.q: What turns sunlight directly into electricity?
18839.e: Solar cells on roofs turn sunlight into electricity. Many solar cells together form a solar power system.
18839.m: Solar cells turn sunlight into electricity.

18840.q: What turns on a wind turbine when the wind blows?
18840.e: The wind turns the large rotor blades. A generator turns this movement into electricity.
18840.m: Wind turbines turn wind into electricity.

18841.q: How can you save energy at home?
a: Switch the light off when you leave
Leave the windows open in winter
Leave the television on all the time
18841.e: Light that nobody needs uses electricity for nothing. If you switch it off, you save energy.
18841.m: Switching off the light saves energy.

18842.q: Which energy source NEVER runs out?
18842.e: Wind is produced again and again, which is why it is called renewable. There is only a limited amount of oil, coal and natural gas.
18842.m: Wind is a renewable energy source.

18843.q: What happens to the energy when a lamp is shining?
a: Electricity turns into light and heat
18843.e: Energy is not lost; it is converted. A lamp turns electricity into light and also some heat.
18843.m: Energy is converted and does not disappear.

18844.q: Which device do you use at school to measure a force?
18844.e: A spring balance contains a spring that stretches more when the force is bigger. You read the force off the scale.
18844.m: A spring balance shows the force by how far a spring stretches.

18845.q: What can a force do to a body?
a: It can change its shape or its movement
It can only change its colour
It can only lower its temperature
18845.e: You can recognise forces by their effects: a body is changed in shape, sped up, slowed down or turned in another direction.
18845.m: Forces change the shape of bodies or change their movement.

18846.q: What does the principle of action and reaction say?
a: Every force has an equal opposite force
18846.e: According to Newton's third law: if one body exerts a force on a second body, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.
18846.m: Every force comes with an equal opposite force.

18847.q: Two children pull on a rope in opposite directions, one with 300 N and one with 250 N. What is the resultant force?
18847.e: With opposite forces you subtract one from the other: 300 N minus 250 N equals 50 N. The rope moves towards the stronger child.
18847.m: Opposite forces are subtracted from each other.

18848.q: What fully describes a force in a drawing?
a: An arrow with direction, length and point of application
A dotted line without a direction
18848.e: A force has a size, a direction and a point where it acts. That is why it is drawn as an arrow.

18849.q: What is the base unit of mass in the International System of Units?
18849.e: The kilogram (kg) is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units (SI).

18850.q: How does an astronaut's mass change when they are on the moon?
18850.e: Mass tells you how much matter a body has. This amount does not change when the body is taken to another place.
18850.m: The mass of a body is the same everywhere.

18851.m: A kilogram has a thousand grams.

18852.q: Roughly what is the mass of 1 litre of water?
18852.e: One litre of water has a mass of about 1 kg, because water has a density of about 1 g per cubic centimetre.
18852.m: One litre of water weighs about one kilogram.

18853.q: Which device measures a mass in a way that does not depend on the place?
18853.e: A beam balance compares the mass with known masses. Because both sides are pulled equally strongly, this works the same everywhere.
18853.m: A beam balance compares masses with each other.

18854.q: What does the inertia of a body mean?
a: It tends to keep its state of motion
It gets heavier and heavier over time
18854.e: A body stays at rest or keeps moving steadily as long as no force acts on it. The greater its mass, the greater its inertia.
18854.m: Bodies with a large mass are hard to accelerate.

18855.q: On Earth, roughly what is the weight of a body with a mass of 1 kg?
18855.e: The gravitational field strength on Earth is around 9.81 N/kg. So one kilogram has a weight of about 9.81 N.
18855.m: On Earth, one kilogram is pulled with about ten newtons.

18856.q: A rucksack has a mass of 5 kg. What is its weight on Earth if you calculate with 10 N/kg?
18856.e: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength = 5 kg × 10 N/kg = 50 N.
18856.m: Weight is mass times gravitational field strength.

18857.q: Why does an astronaut weigh less on the moon than on Earth?
a: Because the moon pulls on them more weakly
Because there is no air on the moon
18857.e: The moon has much less mass than the Earth and therefore pulls on bodies much more weakly.
18857.m: Weight is smaller on the moon than on Earth.

18858.q: Which way does weight point on Earth?
a: Towards the centre of the Earth
18858.e: The Earth pulls all bodies towards its centre. That is why objects fall downwards everywhere on Earth.
18858.m: Weight always points towards the centre of the Earth.

18859.q: Roughly what is the gravitational field strength on the moon?
18859.e: On the surface of the moon, the acceleration due to gravity is about 1.62 m/s², so the gravitational field strength is around 1.6 N/kg.
18859.m: The gravitational field strength depends on the celestial body.

18860.q: How do you calculate average speed?
18860.e: Speed tells you what distance a body travels in a certain time: v = s / t.
18860.m: Speed is distance divided by time.

18861.q: A train travels 240 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
18861.m: For speed you divide the distance by the time.

18862.e: To convert m/s into km/h, you multiply by 3.6. So 10 m/s × 3.6 = 36 km/h.
18862.m: Metres per second times 3.6 gives kilometres per hour.

18863.q: Roughly how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
18863.e: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s, so around 300,000 km per second.
18863.m: Nothing is faster than light in a vacuum.

18864.q: A cyclist rides at 18 km/h. How far does he get in 20 minutes?
18864.e: 20 minutes is a third of an hour. s = v × t = 18 km/h × 1/3 h = 6 km.

a: The speed always stays the same
18865.e: In uniform motion, a body travels equal distances in equal times.
18865.m: In uniform motion the speed does not change.

18866.e: Acceleration is the change in speed per unit of time. Braking is also an acceleration, just in the opposite direction.
18866.m: Acceleration means change in speed per unit of time.

18867.q: In which unit is acceleration measured?
18867.e: Acceleration is change in speed (m/s) divided by time (s). This gives metres per second squared.
18867.m: Acceleration is measured in metres per second squared.

18868.q: A car accelerates from a standstill to 20 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its average acceleration?
18868.e: a = change in speed / time = 20 m/s / 5 s = 4 m/s².
18868.m: Acceleration is the change in speed divided by the time.

18869.q: A bike brakes steadily from 8 m/s to a standstill in 4 seconds. What is its deceleration?
18869.e: The speed falls by 8 m/s in 4 s. Deceleration = 8 m/s / 4 s = 2 m/s².
18869.m: When braking steadily, the speed falls by the same amount every second.

18870.q: Which relationship does Newton's second law describe?
18870.e: The fundamental law of mechanics is F = m × a. For the same mass, a larger force produces a larger acceleration.
18870.m: The larger the force, the more strongly a body is accelerated.

18871.q: What force acts on a cart with a mass of 200 kg that is accelerated at 2 m/s²?

18872.q: How does friction act on a moving body?
18872.e: Friction arises where surfaces touch and move against each other. It acts against the movement.
18872.m: Friction always acts against the movement.

18873.q: Why is grit spread on icy pavements in winter?
a: To make the ice freeze faster
18873.e: Grit makes the surface rougher. This helps the soles of your shoes grip better, so you slip less.

18874.q: Under the same conditions, which type of friction is usually the smallest?
a: They are always all the same
18874.e: That is why we use wheels and ball bearings: rolling creates much less friction than sliding or breaking free from static friction.

18875.q: What does friction produce when you rub your hands together?
18875.e: With friction, kinetic energy is converted into thermal energy. Your hands get warm.

18876.q: What is lubricating oil for on a bike chain?
18876.e: Oil forms a thin film between the metal parts. This makes them slide more easily and wear out less.

18877.q: When is friction wanted and useful?
18877.e: Brakes only work thanks to friction between the brake pad and the rim or disc. Without friction you could not stop.
18877.m: Without friction you could neither walk nor brake.

18878.q: In which unit is energy measured?
18878.e: The SI unit of energy is the joule (J), named after James Prescott Joule.

18879.q: Which form of energy does a rolling ball have?
18879.e: Every moving body has kinetic energy, also called energy of movement.
18879.m: Everything that moves has kinetic energy.

18880.q: Which energy is stored in the water of a reservoir high up in the mountains?
18880.e: Water high up has potential energy. It is greater the greater the mass and height are.
18880.m: The higher a body is, the more potential energy it has.

18881.q: Which form of energy is stored in food?
18881.e: Food contains chemical energy in its molecules. The body obtains it through digestion and respiration.

18882.q: Which form of energy does sunlight carry to the Earth?
18882.e: The sun gives off electromagnetic radiation. This radiant energy reaches the Earth even through empty space.
18882.m: Sunlight brings radiant energy to the Earth.

18883.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a hydroelectric power station?
18883.e: The water flows down from above and drives a turbine, and a generator produces electricity. In Switzerland, more than half of the electricity produced in the country comes from hydropower (as of 2024).
18883.m: Hydroelectric power stations make electricity from falling water.

18884.q: Which conversion happens in a solar cell?
18884.e: A solar cell (photovoltaic cell) converts the radiant energy of light directly into electrical energy.
18884.m: Solar cells convert light into electricity.

18885.q: What happens to the energy when a bouncing ball bounces lower and lower?
18885.e: Each time it hits the ground, some of the energy is converted into heat and sound. This energy is then missing for the height.
18885.m: Some energy is often given off as heat.

18886.q: Which conversion takes place in an electric motor?
18886.e: In an electric motor, the current produces magnetic fields that make the motor turn. A generator does the opposite.
18886.m: An electric motor turns electricity into movement.

18887.q: What does the efficiency of a machine tell you?
a: What proportion of the energy is usefully converted
18887.e: Efficiency is the ratio of useful energy to energy supplied. It is always less than 100 per cent.
18887.m: No machine has an efficiency of a hundred per cent.

18888.q: In which unit is voltage measured?
18888.e: Voltage is measured in volts (V), named after Alessandro Volta.

18889.q: In which unit is electric current measured?
18889.e: Current is measured in amperes (A), named after André-Marie Ampère.

18890.q: What is the mains voltage of ordinary sockets in Switzerland?
18890.e: In Switzerland and Europe, ordinary household sockets supply an alternating voltage of 230 volts at 50 hertz.
18890.m: Household sockets in Switzerland have 230 volts.

18891.q: Which particles move in a metal wire when electricity flows?
18891.e: In metals, electrons can move freely. When a voltage is applied, they travel through the wire.
18891.m: Electricity in metals is a movement of electrons.

18892.q: How do two negatively charged bodies behave towards each other?
a: They have no effect on each other
18892.e: Like charges push each other away, unlike charges attract each other.
18892.m: Like charges push each other away.

18894.q: What is the minimum needed for a bulb in a circuit to light up?
a: A voltage source and a closed circuit
A magnet and a battery without wires
18894.e: Electricity can only flow if the circuit from the voltage source through the bulb and back to the source is closed.
18894.m: Electricity only flows in a closed circuit.

18895.q: What happens in a series circuit of bulbs if one bulb blows?
18895.e: In a series circuit there is only one path for the current. If it is broken, no current flows anywhere any more.
18895.m: In a series circuit, one fault breaks the whole circuit.

18896.q: Why are the lights in a flat connected in parallel?
a: So that each light works on its own
So that they all go out at the same time
So that fewer cables are needed
So that the electricity flows more slowly
18896.e: In a parallel circuit, every appliance has its own path for the current and the full mains voltage. If one fails, the others keep working.
18896.m: In a parallel circuit, every appliance works independently.

18897.e: Ohm's law links voltage U, resistance R and current I. With the same resistance, the current rises with the voltage.
18897.m: With the same resistance, more voltage means more current.

18898.q: A current of 0.05 A flows through a resistance of 100 ohms. What is the voltage?

a: A direct connection of the terminals without anything using the electricity
A bulb with a short life
18899.e: In a short circuit, the current flows with almost no resistance. The current becomes very large and cables can get hot. Fuses then switch off.
18899.m: A short circuit is dangerous because a very large current flows.

18900.q: Which material conducts electricity very well?
18900.e: Copper is a metal with a very low electrical resistance. That is why most electric cables are made of copper.

18901.q: Which material is a good electrical insulator?
18901.e: Plastic has practically no charge carriers that can move freely. That is why cables are covered with plastic.
18901.m: Insulators do not let electricity through.

18902.e: Graphite is made of carbon and has charge carriers that can move freely. That is why it conducts electricity, even though it is not a metal.
18902.m: Some non-metals such as graphite also conduct electricity.

18903.q: Why must you not touch electrical appliances with wet hands?
a: Because water switches the electricity off
Because water is a perfect insulator
Because the appliances would otherwise rust
18903.e: Tap water contains dissolved salts and therefore conducts electricity. Wet skin greatly reduces the body's resistance.
18903.m: Water and electricity are a dangerous combination.

18904.q: What are the insulators on high-voltage pylons traditionally often made of?
18904.e: Porcelain and glass are very good insulators and weatherproof. They stop electricity flowing from the line into the pylon.
18904.m: Porcelain and glass insulate very well.

18905.q: What do you call materials such as silicon whose conductivity lies between that of conductors and insulators?
18905.e: Semiconductors such as silicon are the basis of computer chips, light-emitting diodes and solar cells.
18905.m: Computer chips are made of semiconductors.

18906.q: How do two like magnetic poles behave towards each other?
18906.e: Like poles, that is north and north or south and south, push each other away. Unlike poles attract each other.
18906.m: Like magnetic poles push each other away.

18907.q: Which metal is attracted by a magnet?
18907.e: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic and are attracted by magnets. Copper, aluminium and gold are not.

18908.q: Why does a compass needle point roughly north?
a: Because it lines up with the Earth's magnetic field
Because it is attracted by the sun
Because the North Pole is colder
18908.e: The Earth has a magnetic field. The compass needle is a small magnet and lines up with this field.
18908.m: A compass lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.

18909.q: How can you make magnetic field lines visible?
18909.e: Iron filings briefly become magnetic themselves and line up along the field lines.
18909.m: Iron filings show the shape of magnetic fields.

18910.q: What forms around a wire that electricity is flowing through?
18910.e: In 1820 the Danish physicist Hans Christian Ørsted discovered that a wire carrying a current makes a compass needle move.
18910.m: Electric current produces a magnetic field.

18911.q: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?
a: Use more turns and an iron core
Build the coil out of wood
Make the wire shorter and use only one turn
18911.e: More turns, a higher current and an iron core make the magnetic field of a coil stronger.
18911.m: An iron core strengthens the magnetic field of a coil.

18912.q: Roughly how fast does sound travel in air at 20 °C?
18912.e: In dry air at 20 °C, the speed of sound is about 343 metres per second, which is around 1,200 km/h.
18912.m: In air, sound travels around one kilometre in three seconds.

18913.q: Why can you not hear sound in space?
a: Because there is no air there to carry it
Because it is too cold there
Because the stars are too loud
18913.e: Sound is a vibration of particles and needs something to carry it, such as air, water or solids. In a vacuum there is nothing like that.
18913.m: Sound needs a material to travel through.

18914.q: What do you call the number of vibrations per second of a sound?
18914.e: Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz). The higher the frequency, the higher the sound.
18914.m: High notes have a high frequency.

18915.q: In which unit is sound level given?
18915.e: Sound level is given in decibels (dB). An increase of 10 dB sounds roughly twice as loud.

18916.q: What do you call sound with frequencies above 20,000 Hz, which humans cannot hear?
18916.e: Ultrasound is above the range of human hearing. Bats use it to find their way, and doctors use it to make pictures of the inside of the body.
18916.m: Bats find their way using ultrasound.

18917.q: You see lightning and hear the thunder 6 seconds later. Roughly how far away is the storm?
18917.e: Sound takes about 3 seconds to travel a kilometre. 6 s divided by 3 s per km gives about 2 km.
18917.m: The seconds until the thunder divided by three give roughly the distance in kilometres.

18918.q: What happens to a ray of light when it passes at an angle from air into water?
18918.e: Light is slower in water than in air. When it passes from one to the other at an angle, it is therefore bent towards the normal.
18918.m: Light changes direction when it passes into another material.

18919.q: Why does a straw in a glass of water look bent?
a: Because of the refraction of light
Because of the sound in the glass
18919.e: The light from the part of the straw under water is bent as it leaves the water surface. The eye traces the rays back in a straight line.
18919.m: Refraction makes objects in water appear shifted.

18920.q: What does a converging lens (convex lens) do with parallel rays of light?
a: It brings them together at a focal point
It spreads them in all directions
18920.e: A converging lens is thicker in the middle than at the edge. Parallel rays are refracted so that they meet at the focal point.

18921.q: Which piece of glass splits white light into the colours of the rainbow?
18921.e: In a prism, light is refracted twice. Violet light is refracted more strongly than red light, which creates a colour spectrum.
18921.m: White light is made up of many colours.

18922.e: With short-sightedness, the image forms in front of the retina. A diverging lens (concave lens) moves the focal point further back.

18923.q: What does the law of reflection say?
a: The angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are equal
The angle of reflection is always 90 degrees
Light is always reflected back to the light source
The angle of incidence is twice as large
18923.e: Both angles are measured from the normal, the line at right angles to the mirror surface. They are always equal.
18923.m: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

18924.q: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 35 degrees to the normal. What is the angle between the incoming and the reflected ray?
18924.e: The reflected ray also makes 35 degrees with the normal, but on the other side. Together that makes 35 + 35 = 70 degrees.
18924.m: The angle between the two rays is twice the angle of incidence.

18925.q: How does an image appear in a flat mirror?
18925.e: A flat mirror swaps front and back. That is why the image looks reversed, for example your right hand appears as a left hand.
18925.m: In a mirror everything appears reversed left to right.

18926.q: Why can we see objects that do not give off light themselves?
a: Because our eyes send out light
18926.e: Objects that do not glow reflect part of the light that hits them. This light reaches our eyes.
18926.m: We see things because they reflect light into our eyes.

18927.q: What is the scattered reflection from a rough surface called?
18927.e: Rough surfaces reflect light in many directions. That is why paper does not act like a mirror but can be seen from everywhere.

18928.q: Why do cyclists wear reflectors at night?
a: So that they reflect the light of headlights
So that they produce electricity themselves
So that the bike goes faster
18928.e: Reflectors send the light from car headlights back towards the light source. This way the driver sees the bike early.
18928.m: Reflectors make you visible in the dark.

18929.e: Pressure tells you how strongly a force is spread over an area: p = F / A.

18930.q: In which unit is pressure measured?
18930.e: One pascal (Pa) equals one newton per square metre. Bar or hectopascal are also often used.

18931.q: Why do you sink less deeply into the snow with snowshoes?
a: Because the force is spread over a larger area
18931.e: The weight stays the same, but the contact area becomes larger. This makes the pressure on the snow smaller.
18931.m: A large area reduces the pressure.

18932.q: A crate exerts a force of 600 N on an area of 2 m². What is the pressure?
18932.m: Pressure is force divided by area.

18933.q: How does water pressure change as you dive deeper?
18933.e: The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you. For every 10 m of water depth, the pressure rises by about 1 bar.
18933.m: The deeper in the water, the greater the pressure.

18934.q: At what temperature does pure water boil at normal air pressure?
18934.e: At an air pressure of 1013 hPa, pure water boils at 100 °C. Celsius based his scale on the freezing and boiling points of water.
18934.m: At sea level, water boils at a hundred degrees Celsius.

18935.q: Why does water boil at less than 100 °C in the mountains?
a: Because the air pressure is lower there
Because the water is purer there
18935.e: The lower the air pressure, the lower the boiling temperature. At about 3000 m, water already boils at around 90 °C.
18935.m: At low air pressure, water boils sooner.

18936.q: Roughly what is absolute zero in degrees Celsius?
18936.e: Absolute zero is exactly -273.15 °C. There the particles have the lowest possible energy; it cannot get any colder.
18936.m: Nothing can be colder than absolute zero.

18937.e: You calculate K = °C + 273.15. So 20 + 273.15 = 293.15 K, about 293 K.
18937.m: For kelvin, add 273 to the degrees Celsius.

18938.q: What happens to the particles of a substance when its temperature rises?
18938.e: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. The warmer it is, the more vigorously they move.

18939.q: Why do bridges have expansion joints?
a: Because bridges would otherwise be too heavy
So that rainwater can drain away
So that cars drive more slowly
18939.e: Most substances expand when heated and contract when cold. Expansion joints prevent cracks.

19040.q: At how many degrees does water boil at sea level?
19040.e: At sea level, pure water starts to boil at 100 degrees Celsius. High up in the mountains it boils at a little less than 100 degrees.
19040.m: At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees.

19041.q: What colour is clean water in a glass?
19041.e: Clean water is clear and see-through. You can look through a glass of water.
19041.m: Clean water is clear and see-through.

19042.q: What does clean drinking water smell of?
19042.e: Pure water has no smell and no taste. If water smells strange, you should not drink it.

19043.q: Where does most of the drinking water in Switzerland come from?
19043.e: In Switzerland, about 80 per cent of drinking water comes from springs and groundwater. The rest comes mainly from lakes.
19043.m: Most Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.

19044.q: What happens to a puddle on a hot day?
19044.e: The sun warms the water, and it slowly goes into the air as invisible vapour. That is how the puddle disappears.
19044.m: Puddles dry up in the sun.

19045.q: What is water like at room temperature?
19045.e: At room temperature water is liquid. You can pour it and drink it.
19045.m: At room temperature water is liquid.

19046.q: Where on Earth is there the most water?
19046.e: Almost all the water on Earth is salt water in the seas. Fresh water in rivers and lakes is only a small part.
19046.m: Most of the Earth’s water is in the seas.

19047.q: What do we call water that falls from the clouds?
19047.e: When the droplets in a cloud get too heavy, they fall down. That is rain.
19047.m: Rain is water that falls from clouds.

19048.e: Air is see-through and has no colour. But you can feel it, for example as wind.
19048.m: Air is invisible, but you can feel it.

19049.q: What is inside a blown-up balloon?
19049.e: When you blow up a balloon, you blow air into it. The air pushes the skin of the balloon outwards.
19049.m: A blown-up balloon is filled with air.

19050.q: Which part of the air do we need to breathe?
19050.e: Our body needs the oxygen in the air. We breathe it in with every breath.
19050.m: We need oxygen from the air to breathe.

19051.q: What is air mostly made of?
19051.e: About four fifths of air is nitrogen. The rest is mainly other gases.
19051.m: Air is mostly made of nitrogen.

19052.q: What happens if you push an empty glass upside down into water?
19052.e: There is air in the “empty” glass. It takes up space and does not let all the water in.
19052.m: Air takes up space, even though you cannot see it.

19053.q: Where does the air get thinner?
19053.e: The higher you climb, the less air there is. That is why mountaineers find it harder to breathe on high peaks.
19053.m: The air is thinner high up in the mountains.

19054.q: What does a fire need to burn?
19054.e: A fire needs something that can burn, oxygen from the air and enough heat. If one of these is missing, it goes out.
19054.m: Fire needs fuel, air and heat.

19055.q: What happens to a candle if you put a glass over it?
19055.e: Under the glass, the oxygen runs out. Without enough oxygen, the flame goes out.
19055.m: Without fresh air a flame goes out.

19056.q: What is left when wood has burnt completely?
19056.e: When wood burns, most of it turns into gas and smoke. Grey ash is left behind.
19056.m: Ash is left over from burnt wood.

19057.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland if there is a fire?
19057.e: In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118. 117 is the police and 144 is the ambulance.
19057.m: In Switzerland the fire brigade’s number is 118.

19058.q: What does a fire give off?
19058.e: A flame shines and is hot. That is why people like sitting round a campfire.
19058.m: Fire gives off light and warmth.

19059.q: What happens when wet wood burns?
19059.e: Wet wood burns badly and makes lots of smoke. Dry wood burns better.
19059.m: Wet wood makes lots of smoke when it burns.

19060.q: Who is allowed to light a fire?
a: Only adults, or children with them
Little brothers and sisters on their own
19060.e: Fire is dangerous and can spread quickly. Children only light fires together with adults.
19060.m: Children only light fires with adults.

19061.e: When water gets very cold, it becomes solid. We call this solid water ice.

19062.q: Does an ice cube float in water or sink?
19062.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of liquid water. That is why it floats on top.

19063.e: Ice is solid and therefore hard. It cools everything it touches.

19064.q: What is glacier ice made from?
19064.e: Lots of snow is pressed together over many years. This turns it into solid glacier ice.
19064.m: Glacier ice is made from snow that has been pressed together.

19065.q: Why is a frozen lake dangerous?
19065.e: Thin ice cannot hold a person’s weight. You may only go onto ice that has been declared safe.
19065.m: Only go onto a frozen lake when the ice has been declared safe.

19066.q: Where do you put water to make ice cubes?
19066.e: In the freezer it is much colder than 0 degrees. The water turns to ice there.
19066.m: You make ice cubes in the freezer.

19067.q: What rises from a saucepan of boiling water?
19067.e: Boiling water turns into water vapour. The white clouds above it are tiny droplets of water.

19068.q: Why do you have to be careful with steam?
19068.e: Steam from boiling water is very hot. It can scald your skin.
19068.m: Hot steam can scald your skin.

19069.q: What happens to steam on a cold mirror in the bathroom?
19069.e: The steam cools down on the cold mirror. It turns back into little drops of water, and the mirror steams up.
19069.m: Steam turns back into water on cold surfaces.

19070.e: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They form when moist air cools down.
19070.m: Clouds are made of tiny water droplets.

19071.q: What do you see in winter when you breathe out outside?
19071.e: Our breath contains water vapour. In the cold air it turns into tiny droplets, which you see as a white cloud.
19071.m: In winter you can see your breath as a little cloud.

19072.q: Where does the steam go when you cook?
19072.e: Warm steam is lighter than the cool air. That is why it rises.

19073.q: What forms when steam collects on the saucepan lid?
19073.e: The lid is cooler than the steam. So the steam turns back into water there and drips down.
19073.m: On the lid, steam turns back into drops of water.

19074.q: Which of these is a solid?
19074.e: A stone has a fixed shape and stays the way it is. Milk, juice and air are not solid.

19075.q: What is typical of a solid?
19075.e: Solids have their own shape. A wooden block stays a block, whatever box it is in.

19076.q: Which of these objects is solid?
19076.e: Wood is a solid. Soup and syrup are liquid, and fog is made of air and droplets.

19077.e: Sand can trickle, but every single grain is solid. That is why sand counts as a solid.
19077.m: Every grain of sand is solid.

19078.q: Which solid is hard and see-through?
19078.e: Window panes are made of glass. Glass is solid and hard, and you can see through it.
19078.m: Glass is a solid that is see-through.

19079.q: Which of these is a solid?
19079.e: Cold chocolate is hard and keeps its shape. Tea and juice are liquid, and steam is a gas.

19080.q: Can you hold a solid in your hand?
19080.e: You can hold solids because they do not flow away. A cube stays a cube in your hand.
19080.m: You can hold solids in your hand.

19081.q: Which of these is a liquid?
19081.e: You can pour milk, and it flows. Wood, stone and glass are solid.

19082.q: What shape is water in a bottle?
19082.e: Liquids do not have their own shape. They take the shape of the container they are in.
19082.m: Liquids take the shape of their container.

19083.q: What can you do with a liquid?
19083.e: Liquids flow. That is why you can pour them from one glass into another.

19084.q: Which of these flows most slowly?
19084.e: Honey is thick. It flows much more slowly than water, juice or milk.
19084.m: Honey is thick and flows slowly.

19085.q: What is the surface of water like in a glass that is standing still?
19085.e: Still water forms a flat, level surface at the top. This is true of all liquids.
19085.m: Still water has a flat surface on top.

19086.q: What happens if you spill water on the table?
19086.e: Water has no fixed shape. On the table it flows apart and forms a puddle.

19087.q: Which oil do you often find in the kitchen?
19087.e: In the kitchen you use cooking oil for frying and for salad. It is a liquid.
19087.m: Cooking oil is a liquid from the kitchen.

19088.q: Which of these is a gas?
19088.e: Air is a gas. It is invisible and spreads out everywhere in a room.

19089.q: What does a gas do in a room?
19089.e: Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume. They spread out through the whole room.
19089.m: Gases spread out through the whole room.

19090.q: How can you tell that there is a gas in the room that you cannot see?
19090.e: Many gases are invisible. But some have a smell, for example the scent of freshly baked bread.
